newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan poised to make progress in talks.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan poised to make progress in talks.

text.p: Longtime bitter foes, India and Pakistan are the closest in years to narrowing differences as they glimpse the economic benefits of lasting peace and an end to a military standoff in Kashmir, diplomats say.
In an ironic twist, Pakistan's economic troubles and India's economic growth are nudging the two sides towards each other.
Nearly 50 years of squabbling over Kashmir have sapped the South Asian neighbours' exchequers and left their armies face-to-face across a line dividing the Himalayan region.
Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif said in Islamabad on Tuesday that the conflict could only be resolved through talks.
"Dialogue is a must because without a dialogue we really can't move ahead, we can't think of resolving the problems between India and Pakistan," he told reporters.
The resumption of talks between the two nations' foreign secretaries this week in the Indian capital provides the best chance in three years to reduce tension, diplomats said.
"We think there are modestly good prospects for progress," a senior Western diplomat said.
"But both sides have the capacity to bungle things because of vigorous and narrow-minded constituencies if they don't handle things with extreme care and diplomacy," he said.
As ever, the main sticking point is Kashmir -- a mostly Moslem region which has been divided between the two countries since shortly after their birth as independent states in 1947.
The last foreign secretary-level talks in 1994 bogged down over Kashmir as Pakistan insisted that it be the main focus of negotiations. India wanted a broader negotiating palette.
"They have to find a way to get out of the gravity well of Kashmir. If it is the centre of the solar system, it is difficult to look at anything else," one envoy said.
But diplomats said Pakistan may have lost hope of capitalising on a separatist insurgency which has racked India's Jammu and Kashmir state since 1990.
India held local elections in the state last September and claims the militants are on the run. Pakistan has had difficulty drawing international opprobrium on to India over the issue.
"India is in a position of strength in Kashmir," a diplomat said. "Pakistan knows it has lost Kashmir, both on the ground and internationally."
Provided a face-saving formula can be found, India and Pakistan might be able to follow up on recent conciliatory gestures and take new confidence-building steps.
Earlier this month Pakistan freed 38 Indian children held along with adult fishermen. India followed by relaxing travel restrictions on Pakistani visitors.
Diplomats are looking to Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral to apply what has become known as the Gujral Doctrine to Pakistan.

Gujral, who was expected to meet his Pakistani counterpart, Gohar Ayub Khan, on the margins of a Non-Aligned Movement meeting in New Delhi on April 7-8, has made gestures to both Bangladesh and Nepal which have radically improved ties.

"Because India is a big country, it can afford to go more than half-way without expecting reciprocity and make big political gestures and reap the benefits downstream," one envoy said, describing Gujral's approach.
New Delhi might be ready to withdraw troops from the Siachen glacier in Kashmir and make trade concessions.
"It is very clear that India is prepared to move very quickly on Siachen and the economy," a diplomat said.

Indian trade concessions could sooth Pakistan's economic woes. Said a diplomat: "Pakistan's economy is in serious trouble, it has to be the priority. It almost necessitates an improvement in relations, quite possibly progress towards a solution in Kashmir."

Long resistant to putting Kashmir aside, Islamabad might be more willing to talk on parallel tracks and participate in working groups which would focus on well-defined problems, including border disputes and trade, diplomats said.
